title: IndyCar on the National Mall: A Thrill Ride or a Risk to National Treasures?
summary:
This Sunday, more than two dozen IndyCar drivers will tear around a 1.7-mile track on Washington, D.C.'s National Mall at speeds up to 180 mph. The Freedom 250 Grand Prix, part of the nation's 250th birthday celebration, will send cars hurtling past the National Gallery of Art, the National Archives, and three Smithsonian museums. It's an unprecedented event—and it has sparked a fierce debate over whether the roar of engines could literally shake the foundations of American cultural heritage.

The National Gallery of Art has already boarded up outdoor sculptures in its garden, which sits directly along the course. Spokesperson Chris Abanavas told NPR the museum conducted an extensive vibration study and implemented measures to ensure safety. But neither the National Archives nor the Smithsonian answered NPR's questions about their preparations.

Race organizers—the White House and IndyCar, owned by Penske Entertainment Corp.—insist they've followed all protocols. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said they've been in close coordination with relevant agencies to ensure the "safest and most secure race." IndyCar points to other races in sensitive areas: one in Detroit's Belle Isle Park and another that speeds past the Dalí Museum in St. Petersburg, Florida. Beth Bell, the Dalí's chief marketing officer, noted the museum was built to withstand a Category 5 hurricane and has remained safe throughout the event's history.

But critics argue the National Mall is fundamentally different. Speed limits there are typically 25 mph. No modern race has ever been held on this hallowed ground—only centuries-old horse races. And organizers had less than a year to plan. Art historian Mary Okin, assistant director at Living New Deal, is particularly concerned about the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building, a protected historic site with murals inside. She wrote to the National Park Service warning of potential damage from vibrations, fires, and flying debris.

"For several hours of racing cars, we might be risking the access to these extraordinary works for future generations," Okin told NPR. She sees the race as part of a broader pattern of the administration disregarding historic preservation. The National Park Service, Department of the Interior, and Department of Transportation did not respond to NPR's inquiries.

As engines rev and crowds gather, the question remains: is the thrill of the race worth the potential cost to the nation's irreplaceable treasures?
why_it_matters: This story shows how public celebrations can clash with the duty to protect cultural resources for the future; the decision-making around the race may set a precedent for what kinds of high-speed events are allowed on protected civic land.

background_read: The National Mall is the historic park in downtown Washington, D.C., that connects the U.S. Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and is lined with memorials and museums central to American civic life.

The National Gallery of Art is a major art museum on the Mall; the National Archives keeps founding documents such as the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights; and the Smithsonian Institution is the world's largest museum, education, and research complex.
In the 19th century parts of the Mall were used informally, but modern planners generally restrict high-speed activity there to protect monuments, museum collections, and public safety.

Race organizers point to street races in Detroit and St. Petersburg as evidence that cars can safely pass near cultural sites, but preservationists argue those settings are not identical to a national memorial landscape.
This debate reflects a wider question about who gets to decide how protected civic spaces are used, especially when the event is tied to a national celebration.

perspectives.description: Race organizers and many spectators see the Freedom 250 Grand Prix as an exciting, once-in-a-lifetime way to mark the nation's 250th birthday. They argue that officials have conducted safety studies and that other urban races near museums have gone forward without major damage.

Art historians and preservation advocates worry that the event prioritizes spectacle over the long-term safety of irreplaceable museums and historic structures. Mary Okin, for example, warns that vibrations, fire, and flying debris could endanger murals and protected buildings, and she sees the decision as part of a wider disregard for historic preservation.

The conflict highlights a risk-management problem: cultural institutions can board up sculptures and study vibrations, but they cannot fully guarantee that old buildings and delicate artworks will be unharmed. Because several federal agencies did not answer press inquiries, outside observers lack the data needed to evaluate the real level of risk.

The unanswered questions from the National Park Service, Department of the Interior, and Department of Transportation leave an accountability gap. If the race proceeds without transparent safety data, future events on the Mall may face stronger legal or public opposition, but if it succeeds, it could open the door to more commercial uses of protected civic space.
